questions.question: Let $D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ be convex and let $f\colon D\to\mathbb{R}$ be quasi-convex with a global minimum on $D$, minimum value $m$. Which property of $V_{\mathrm{min}}=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in D\colon f(\boldsymbol{x})=m\}$ is guaranteed?
options: $V_{\mathrm{min}}$ consists of exactly one point of $D$.
$V_{\mathrm{min}}$ is nonempty, convex and closed.
$V_{\mathrm{min}}$ is nonempty and convex.
$V_{\mathrm{min}}$ is nonempty, convex and bounded.

questions.question: Let $f$ be quasi-convex on a convex set $D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ with global minimum value $m$. Which description of $V_{\mathrm{min}}=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in D\colon f(\boldsymbol{x})=m\}$ shows directly that this set is convex?
options: $V_{\mathrm{min}}=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in D\colon f(\boldsymbol{x})\leq m\}$, since no value of $f$ lies below $m$.
$V_{\mathrm{min}}=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in D\colon f(\boldsymbol{x})<m\}$, the strict sublevel set at level $m$.
$V_{\mathrm{min}}=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in D\colon f(\boldsymbol{x})\geq m\}$, since every value of $f$ is at least $m$.
$V_{\mathrm{min}}=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in D\colon f(\boldsymbol{x})\leq\alpha\}$ for every level $\alpha\geq m$.

questions.question: Let $g$ be quasi-concave on a convex set $D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ and attain its global maximum value $M$ on $D$. Which observation lets the result on minimizers of quasi-convex functions show that the maximizers of $g$ form a convex set?
options: $-g$ is quasi-concave and attains its minimum $-M$ exactly at the maximizers of $g$.
$-g$ is quasi-convex and attains its minimum $-M$ exactly at the maximizers of $g$.
$-g$ is quasi-convex and attains its maximum $-M$ exactly at the maximizers of $g$.
$g$ is concave, so $-g$ is convex and attains its minimum $-M$ at the maximizers of $g$.

questions.question: For $f(\boldsymbol{x})=\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}+b$ on a nonempty convex set $V\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$, the affine case of the result on minimizers assumes $\boldsymbol{a}\neq\boldsymbol{0}$. What happens when $\boldsymbol{a}=\boldsymbol{0}$?
options: $f$ has no global minimum on $V$, so the set of minimizers of $f$ is empty.
The minimizers are exactly the extreme points of $V$, where $f$ is lowest.
The minimizers still form $V\cap H$, now for a hyperplane $H$ through the origin.
Every point of $V$ is a minimizer, and the level set $\{f=b\}$ is all of $\mathbb{R}^n$.

questions.question: Let $V\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ be convex and let $f\colon V\to\mathbb{R}$ be quasi-convex with a global minimum on $V$. Which statement about the minimizers of $f$ and the extreme points of $V$ is correct?
options: Every minimizer of $f$ is an extreme point of $V$, since minima occur at corners.
The set of minimizers of $f$ always contains at least one extreme point of $V$.
A minimizer need not be extreme: minimizers can fill a segment with a non-extreme midpoint.
No minimizer is an extreme point of $V$, because the set of minimizers is convex.

questions.question: The function $f(x)=\bigl(\max\{x-1,0\}\bigr)^3$ on $\mathbb{R}$ is nondecreasing, hence quasi-convex. Which set is the set of global minimizers of $f$?
options: $[1,\infty)$

questions.question: A quasi-convex function $f\colon\mathbb{R}^2\to\mathbb{R}$ has global minimum value $-1$, attained at $(0,4)$ and at $(6,1)$. Which point must also be a global minimizer of $f$?

Let $f(\boldsymbol{x})=2x_1-x_2+1$ on the rectangle $V=[0,1]\times[0,2]$, and let $m$ be the minimum value of $f$ on $V$. Which line is $H=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^2\colon f(\boldsymbol{x})=m\}$?
options: $\{\boldsymbol{x}\colon 2x_1-x_2=-2\}$
$\{\boldsymbol{x}\colon 2x_1-x_2=-1\}$
$\{\boldsymbol{x}\colon 2x_1-x_2=2\}$
$\{\boldsymbol{x}\colon 2x_1-x_2=0\}$

questions.question: Let $f(x)=|x^2-4x|$ on $\mathbb{R}$. Which conclusion about quasi-convexity of $f$, together with its reason, is correct?
options: $f$ is quasi-convex, being the absolute value of the convex function $x^2-4x$.
$f$ is not quasi-convex, because a quasi-convex function has only one minimizer.
$f$ is not quasi-convex, because its set of minimizers $\{0,4\}$ is not convex.
$f$ is quasi-convex, because its set of minimizers is the interval $[0,4]$.

questions.question: Let $f(\boldsymbol{x})=\max\{|x_1|,\,|x_2|-1\}$ for $\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^2$. At which points does $f$ attain its smallest value?
options: the segment from $(0,-1)$ to $(0,1)$
the segment from $(-1,0)$ to $(1,0)$

questions.question: Let $g$ be quasi-concave on a convex set $D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ and attain its global minimum on $D$. Which statement about the set of minimizers of $g$ is correct?
options: It is convex, because the minimizers of $g$ are the minimizers of the quasi-convex function $-g$.
It is convex, because every quasi-concave function is also quasi-convex.
It is a single point, because a quasi-concave function has only one minimizer.
It need not be convex: $g(x)=-x^2$ on $[-1,1]$ is minimal exactly at $-1$ and $1$.

questions.question: Let $\boldsymbol{a}\in\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{\boldsymbol{0}\}$, let $V\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ be convex, and let $f(\boldsymbol{x})=\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}+b$ attain its minimum value $m$ on $V$. When is the set of minimizers $C_m=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in V\colon f(\boldsymbol{x})=m\}$ all of $V$?
options: Exactly when $V$ lies in a hyperplane $\{\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}=c\}$, so that $f$ is constant on $V$.
Never, because $\boldsymbol{a}\neq\boldsymbol{0}$ makes $f$ nonconstant, so some point of $V$ lies above level $m$.
Never, because $C_m=V\cap H$ consists of boundary points of $V$ only.
Whenever $C_m$ has more than one point, because $C_m$ is a convex subset of $V$.

questions.question: Let $V\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ be convex and let $f(\boldsymbol{x})=\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}+b$, with $\boldsymbol{a}\neq\boldsymbol{0}$, attain its minimum value $m$ on $V$ without being constant on $V$. How does $H=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n\colon\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}+b=m\}$ lie relative to $V$?
options: $V$ lies in $\{\boldsymbol{x}\colon\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}+b\leq m\}$ and meets $H$, so $H$ supports $V$.
$H$ meets the interior of $V$ and splits $V$ into points above and below level $m$.
$V$ lies in $\{\boldsymbol{x}\colon\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}+b\geq m\}$ and meets $H$, so $H$ supports $V$.
$H$ supports $V$ only when $V$ is compact; otherwise $H$ may cut through $V$.

questions.question: Let $D=[-3,-1]\cup[1,4]$ and $f(x)=x^2$ for $x\in D$. Which statement about the set of global minimizers of $f$ on $D$ is correct?
options: It is $[-1,1]$, since $x^2$ is convex and its sets of minimizers are convex.
It is $\{-1,1\}$, not convex, which is possible because $D$ is not convex.
It is $\{-1,1\}$, which contradicts the result because $x^2$ is convex.
It is $\{0\}$, the point where the derivative $2x$ vanishes.

questions.question: Let $V=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^2\colon x_1\geq0,\ x_2\geq0,\ x_1+2x_2\geq4,\ 3x_1+x_2\geq6\}$ and $f(\boldsymbol{x})=2x_1+4x_2$. Which set is the set of minimizers of $f$ on $V$?
options: the segment from $(0,6)$ to $(\frac{8}{5},\frac{6}{5})$
the segment from $(0,2)$ to $(4,0)$
the segment from $(\frac{8}{5},\frac{6}{5})$ to $(4,0)$

questions.question: Let $g(\boldsymbol{x})=\min\{x_1,x_2\}$, a concave and hence quasi-concave function, on $V=[0,3]\times[0,2]$. Which set is the set of maximizers of $g$ on $V$?
options: $\{(t,2)\colon 2\leq t\leq3\}$
$\{(t,2)\colon 0\leq t\leq3\}$

questions.question: Let $f\colon\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ attain its global minimum, and suppose its set of minimizers is convex. What can be concluded about quasi-convexity of $f$?
options: $f$ is quasi-convex, since a convex set of minimizers characterizes quasi-convexity.
$f$ is quasi-convex provided that it has exactly one minimizer.
$f$ need not be quasi-convex, but it is whenever every sublevel set $\{f\leq\alpha\}$ is bounded.
$f$ need not be quasi-convex: $\min\{|x|,|x-4|+1\}$ has the one minimizer $0$ but is not quasi-convex.

questions.question: Let $f$ be quasi-convex on a convex set $D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ and bounded below, and let $\mu=\inf\{f(\boldsymbol{x})\colon\boldsymbol{x}\in D\}$. Which statement about $S=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in D\colon f(\boldsymbol{x})=\mu\}$ holds for every such $f$?
options: $S$ is nonempty and convex, by the result on sets of minimizers.
$S$ is convex but may be empty, as for $f(x)=\mathrm{e}^{x}$ on $D=\mathbb{R}$.
$S$ is nonempty and convex whenever the domain $D$ is closed.
$S$ is convex if $f$ attains $\mu$, and otherwise $S$ is not convex.

questions.question: Let $V=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^2\colon x_2\geq0,\ x_2\geq x_1-1,\ x_2\geq-x_1-1\}$ and, for a parameter $c\in\mathbb{R}$, $f(\boldsymbol{x})=c\,x_1+x_2$. For which values of $c$ is the set of minimizers of $f$ on $V$ a half-line $\{\boldsymbol{p}+t\boldsymbol{d}\colon t\geq0\}$ with $\boldsymbol{d}\neq\boldsymbol{0}$?
options: Exactly for $c=0$, when $f=x_2$ is minimal along the bottom edge of $V$.
Exactly for $|c|>1$, when $f$ decreases without bound along an edge of $V$.
Exactly for $c=1$ and $c=-1$, when $f$ is constant along an unbounded edge of $V$.
For no value of $c$, since minimizers of an affine function form a corner or an edge between two corners.

questions.question: Let $V=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^2\colon x_2\geq x_1^2,\ x_1\leq1\}$ and $f(\boldsymbol{x})=x_2-4x_1$. Which statement about the minimum of $f$ on $V$ is correct?
options: The minimum value is $-3$, attained only at $(1,1)$.
The minimum value is $-4$, attained only at $(2,4)$.
The minimum value is $-3$, attained on the edge $\{(1,t)\colon t\geq1\}$.
The minimum value is $0$, attained only at the vertex $(0,0)$.
